newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels catch Zaire army off guard, refugees flee.
newsitem.headline: Rebels catch Zaire army off guard, refugees flee.

text.p: Rebel advances in the east have caught Zaire's demoralised army off guard and put tens of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees to flight once again, sources on both sides and relief workers say.

A senior Zairean Defence Ministry official said on Wednesday the army was rushing men and weapons to defend Moba, in the mineral-rich province of Shaba, and Lubutu on the road to Kisangani, the base for its counter-offensive to the north.
But the Tutsi-led rebels say their thrusts on several fronts have stopped the counter-offensive in its tracks and have given President Mobutu Sese Seko until February 21 to stand down.

"We have built a motivated and dedicated army ready to liberate this country from 31 years of looting, plunder and destruction by Mobutu and his cronies," rebel leader Laurent Kabila told reporters at his Goma headquarters in the east.

Kabila, a veteran Mobutu foe, says resistance is weakening, particularly on the approaches to Lubutu, which controls the road to Kisangani, operational headquarters of the army counter- offensive launched on January 20.

The rebel claims could not be independently confirmed but while Kabila says they are fighting alone, the United States has joined a growing chorus of international concern about the role played by Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi in the conflict.
"The United States appeals again to the neighbours of Zaire to stay out of Zaire, to not involve themselves in the fighting," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said in Washington.
Burns stopped short of accusing Rwanda and Uganda of intervening directly in the conflict, as Zaire has done.

But while the debate rages, international relief officials, including U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees Sadako Ogata, spotlight the plight of refugees or Zairean civilians trapped or threatened by the war. Ogata is expected in Zaire on Friday.

The Hutu refugees fled Rwanda fearing reprisals after the 1994 genocide there. They fled again after the Tutsi-led rebels took up arms in earnest in October, accusing the Zairean authorities of denying them citizenship and planning to expel them.

More than 500,000 Hutus walked home after rebels attacked their camps in the east in December but several hundred thousand more streamed west into remote forests along with Hutu hardliners blamed for the genocide.
The rebels and other sources in the region say the Hutu hardliners are fighting alongside the Zairean army.
But many of the refugees who fled with them are clustered in makeshift camps around Lubutu and on the road to Kisangani -- short of food and prey to death and disease.
Further south, an estimated 40,000 Rwandan Hutus fled their camp in Shabunda, where police fired in the air to disperse 150 people surrounding a U.N. relief plane demanding a flight out.
"It seems that reports that Katshunga (45 km or 25 miles to the north east) had fallen to the rebels started the moves," said Ariane Quentier, U.N. spokeswoman in Kinshasa.

Mobutu, said by aides to be returning home after fresh tests in Europe following cancer surgery in August, spent Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday in Morocco, which sent troops to help him crush rebellions in Shaba in the 1970s.
But despite widespread speculation that Zaire was seeking help from friendly nations, there was no confirmation that any was prepared to send troops to fight alongside its army.
